newsitem.title: ROMANIA: SOCCER-STEAUA'S 1986 TRIUMPH UNLIKELY TO BE REPEATED.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-STEAUA'S 1986 TRIUMPH UNLIKELY TO BE REPEATED.

text.p: If Borussia Dortmund beat holders Juventus in Munich next week, it will be the biggest upset in the European Cup final since Steaua Bucharest beat hotly-favoured Barcelona in Seville 11 years ago.
Steaua's penalty shootout win after the teams failed to produce a goal between them in two hours of football was the biggest upset in any European Cup final since the competition began in 1955.
Steaua, who went unbeaten for three years in the Romanian League in the late 1980s, also defied the odds again and returned to the final three years later when they were crushed 4-0 by Milan.

But the current state of soccer in Romania, plus the political changes since the fall of communism in 1989, suggest that it will be many years before Steaua or any other Romanian club team return to such heights.
This season Steaua won just one of their six Champions' League group stage matches and finished bottom of their section.
They may be the best team in the country but standards have dropped dramatically with more than 300 players at varying levels leaving Romanian club sides since 1989 to play across Europe.

The best players have moved to leading clubs in Italy, Spain, England, Germany or the Netherlands and in the past few days Gheorghe Popescu has helped Barcelona win the European Cup Winners' Cup and Dan Petrescu was one of Chelsea's key men when they beat Middlesbrough in the English F.A. Cup final on Saturday.

Three other top players -- Gheorghe Hagi, Adrian Ilie and Iulian Filipescu -- are all leading Galatasaray's bid to win the Turkish title -- and arguably all could be trying to knock Romanian teams out of European competition next season.

Popescu, who was Barcelona's captain in the Cup Winners' Cup final against Paris St Germain in Rotterdam last week, said: "I wanted to win the Cup at any price for Barcelona -- and we still have a chance of winning the Spanish League and the Spanish Cup.
"But, of course, in a way I would be much happier to play in a European final with a Romanian team, that is only natural. Perhaps one day it will happen with me as a trainer or a president."

One of the reasons Steaua were so successful in Europe in the late 1980s was that as the army club they had official backing to hand pick the best players in the country. The fact that one of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's sons was the club's president did not hurt either.
Virtually the entire 1986 team which won the Champions' Cup and the team of 1989 which lost in the final were full internationals -- a stark contrast to the situation today.

When Romania beat Ireland 1-0 in a World Cup qualifier last month, goalkeeper Bogdan Stelea was the only Steaua player in the team. When Romania defeated Liechtenstein 8-0 in March all 11 players were with foreign clubs.
The authorities were equally benevolent to Dinamo Bucharest, the team of the Securitate police force, who have dominated the domestic championship with Steaua.

Today far more questions are asked about how the league is run and it is reeling from an investigation into allegations that the Romanian F.A. has illegally siphoned off transfer money due to the clubs.

Despite this deep unease at national level, the international team are thriving and have just about clinched their place in next year's World Cup finals having won their opening six group qualifiers with a goal tally of 20-0.
But many Romanians feel as though they have not only lost something at domestic level but also lost touch with the national side as well.

Leading commentator Gheorghe Mitroi wrote in the daily Adevarul newspaper earlier this month: "You feel that our national team is not ours any more, and (instead) many European clubs have been taking part in building our national team."
National coach Anghel Iordanescu, who played for Steaua in the 1986 final and was coach when they lost in 1989, said he has to rely on his overseas stars.
"I can't risk playing domestically based players" he said, underlying the low standard of play in the national championship.
There is also another worry for the fans who fear that the Romanian national side could suffer the same sort of decline experienced at domestic level.
Borussia Moenchengladbach midfielder Ionut Lupescu recently refused to play against Ireland, complaining he had spent most of the previous match against Lithuania on the bench.
Striker Florin Raducioiu, one of Romania's stars when they reached the World Cup finals in 1994, now has an Italian passport.
But Hagi, who along with fellow-exile Petrescu played for Steaua in 1989, says he is convinced he will return to Romania when his career ends and probably work as a coach.
"I cannot contemplate a life outside Romania," Hagi said by phone from Turkey. "I know what happiness we gave Romanians by beating Ireland."
Romanian fans should look forward with some optimism to next year's World cup finals in France with their country again likely to reach the last stages of the competition.
But for fans of Steaua and other clubs looking back promises greater satisfaction than the future promises.
